A Short History of the Tarrowmere & Skelby Light Railway
The Tarrowmere & Skelby Light Railway was never a grand affair. It ran for a little under eleven miles, from the slate quays at Tarrowmere up the dale to the market town of Skelby, on a gauge of 2 ft 3 in, and for most of its life it owned no more than four locomotives. Yet for nearly forty years (1898–1936) it carried the slate, the wool, the schoolchildren and the Saturday shoppers of the whole dale, and it is remembered with great affection.
The idea of a railway up the dale was first put forward by Josiah Pellham, owner of the Greyscar slate quarry, who was tired of sending his slate down to the quay by horse and cart over a road that was, in his own words, "a river in winter and a dust-heap in summer". A standard-gauge branch had been surveyed and found far too costly. Pellham therefore turned to the cheaper alternative of a narrow-gauge line built under a Light Railway Order, which allowed lighter rails, sharper curves and ungated level crossings.
Gertrude at Tarrowmere Quay with a train of slate wagons, about 1905. (Society collection)
Construction began in the spring of 1897 under the engineer Edwin Trask, a young man who had learned his trade on the mineral lines further north. The work was done largely by quarrymen laid off during a slack season, and it went quickly. The only heavy engineering was the timber viaduct of nine spans across the River Tarrow at Marrowgill, and the short tunnel, barely sixty yards long, under the churchyard at Nether Skelby.
The line opened to goods traffic in 1898 and to passengers the following summer. The first locomotive, a small 0-4-2 saddle tank built by Harcott & Dunn, was named Gertrude after Pellham's eldest daughter, though the men always called her "Old Gertie". Passengers rode in four-wheeled carriages with wooden seats and no heating, and the journey from one end of the line to the other took fifty-five minutes, including a long stop at Marrowgill while the engine took water.
Year Event Locomotive
1898 Line opened to goods traffic Gertrude (0-4-2ST)
1899 Passenger service begins Skelby Lass (0-4-2ST)
1907 Extension to Greyscar upper quarry Tarrow (0-6-0T)
1914 Taken under Government control (1914–1919) Sir Josiah (2-6-2T)
1931 Passenger service withdrawn Skelby Lass scrapped
1936 Last slate train; line closed Gertrude (0-4-2ST)
The best years were those before the Great War. Slate output at Greyscar reached its peak in 1909, a third locomotive had arrived, and on market days the little trains were so full that the guard was known to lock the doors and collect the fares at Skelby. There was even a refreshment room of sorts at Marrowgill, a wooden hut grandly called the Station Café, where Mrs. Ada Thwaite sold tea, pies and boiled sweets to passengers waiting for the engine to finish taking water.
The war changed everything. In 1914 the line was taken under Government control, along with the quarry, and the men who had built it went off to France; eleven of them did not come back, and their names are on the memorial in Skelby market place. A fourth and much larger engine, Sir Josiah, was delivered that year to work the heavier trains, but she was hard on the light track and was never popular with the platelayers.
Decline came slowly and then all at once. The quarry never recovered the trade it lost during the war, the motor bus reached Skelby in 1924, and the company had no money to renew its worn-out track. By the end of the decade the directors could list their troubles on the fingers of one hand, and the Society's archive holds the minute book in which they did exactly that:
falling slate tonnage from Greyscar, down by more than half since 1909
competition from the Skelby motor bus, which ran from door to door
the Marrowgill viaduct, whose timbers needed complete renewal
two locomotives out of four unfit for service
no reserve fund, and no prospect of raising one
Passenger trains were withdrawn in 1931, and for five more years a single engine worked the slate traffic three days a week. When the quarry itself closed there was nothing left to carry. The last train ran down the dale in the autumn of 1936 behind Old Gertie, hauling eleven empty wagons and a brake van full of railwaymen and their families. Within two years the rails had been lifted and sold for scrap.
Much of the route can still be followed on foot. The trackbed between Tarrowmere and Marrowgill is now a public footpath, the stone abutments of the viaduct stand on either bank of the river, and the tunnel under the churchyard, though bricked up at both ends, is plain to see from the lane. The station building at Skelby survives as a private house, and its owners have kindly allowed the Society to fix a small plaque beside the door.
The bricked-up south portal of Nether Skelby tunnel, photographed by a member in 2001.
The Tarrowmere Narrow Gauge Society was formed to record what remains and to gather memories while there are still people who can supply them. We hold some three hundred photographs, the company's minute books, a quantity of tickets and waybills, and one slate wagon, rescued from a farmyard and now under restoration. If you have photographs, papers or family stories connected with the line, however slight they may seem, the Archivist would be very pleased to hear from you.
